title: Why does cutting onions make you cry?
hook: A whole onion is harmless. The tears are a weapon you switch on yourself.
summary: Cutting an onion mixes sulfur compounds and enzymes that were kept apart, producing a gas that irritates the eyes.
cardText: The knife breaks the onion’s cells and mixes sulfur compounds with an enzyme. Within seconds they form a gas that irritates your eyes, and tears wash it away.

cardBlocks.text: A whole onion doesn’t make you cry. The tears start when the knife breaks its cells and mixes substances that were stored apart: sulfur compounds and an enzyme called alliinase.

Within seconds, a chain of reactions produces a gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. It drifts up to your eyes, irritates nerve endings in the cornea, and your body responds with tears to wash it away. It is thought to be the plant’s defense against animals that eat it. Sharp knives and slow cuts spray fewer droplets of onion juice. Chilling the onion is common advice, but a 2025 study found that chilled onions released more droplets, not fewer.
When you cut an onion, you mix the ingredients of the plant’s chemical defense.

deepDiveBlocks.text: For a long time, alliinase alone was thought to make the irritating gas. In 2002, Japanese researchers reported in the journal Nature a second enzyme, lachrymatory-factor synthase, responsible for the final step of the reaction.
That enzyme competes with another chemical pathway that produces the flavor compounds of fresh onion. Onion varieties that cause fewer tears have since been developed.
Cooking switches the enzymes off. That is why sautéed onions do not sting your eyes and taste sweeter.

They found that chilling onions actually yields a larger volume of droplet ejection, possibly due to the brittleness of plant tissues at lower temperatures (although the authors note more study is needed before any definitive conclusions can be reached).
